memory_candidates.content: Claude Code MCP tool availability rests on two independent axes: registration (which surface makes a server exist/connect: local or user ~/.claude.json, or project .mcp.json) and permission (which settings file grants its tools without prompting). A recurring, verifiable failure mode is scope mismatch: a server registered at user scope (machine-wide) but only granted permission inside per-project extension settings-fragment.json files that merge into project-local settings.local.json. This leaves every project lacking that specific extension prompting/denying on every call. Fix: grant permissions at the SAME scope where the server is registered (user-scope registration -> grant in ~/.claude/settings.json; project-scope registration -> grant in the owning extension's settings-fragment.json). Verified concrete example in this repo: playwright (user-scope registered, but grants only in web/present extension fragments, absent from ~/.claude/settings.json) vs. lean-lsp (user-scope registered AND user-scope granted -- the correct pattern).

An mcpServers key inside settings.json/settings.local.json (or an extension's settings-fragment.json, which merges into it) has zero effect in Claude Code -- it never registers a server. The only registration surfaces are ~/.claude.json (local/user scope) and .mcp.json (project scope). A manifest.json's mcp_servers field is an equally dead, independent third copy of the same non-registering declaration; when auditing one dead mcpServers block, check the extension's manifest.json for a parallel dead mcp_servers field too -- both need cleanup, not just the settings-fragment one.

Before treating a task brief's quoted claim as literally present in a target file, grep for the exact substrings first. In this case, a brief described a doc's 'central premise' as a specific quoted justification, but the doc contained zero matches for any of the load-bearing terms (.mcp.json, project-scoped, subagent) -- the actual claim lived in a different, out-of-scope file (a script's header comment) that the doc merely links to. The doc's real defect was an omission (never mentioning a legitimate registration surface at all) with the same practical effect, not the literal sentence described. Always verify a brief's factual claims against the file before planning edits around them.
